notes.short: Hearts, ears, eyes, then eyes, ears, hearts
notes.about: Three words go out in one order and come back in the reverse order: hearts, ears, eyes, then eyes, ears, hearts.

lines.words: Make the hearts of this people calloused;
deafen their ears
and close their eyes.
Otherwise they might see with their eyes,
hear with their ears,
understand with their hearts,

defined.quote: The Repetition of the same Words in an inverse Order (but same Sense)
defined.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

original.note: In Hebrew the ears and the eyes are the same words both times; the heart is lev, then its fuller form, levav.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists this verse under Epanodos, the same words repeated in inverse order, and again under introverted parallelism. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) and Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) both point out the reversed order. Fausset, following Bengel, reads it as corruption flowing from the heart into the ears and eyes, and healing reaching the heart through them.
notes.limit: Writers agree the order is reversed; what the reversal means is one reading, not a settled one.

cites.quote: After two, three, or more words have been mentioned, they are repeated, not in the same order again, but backward.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: In the first member of the sentence, the order is, the heart, ears, eyes; in the latter, the reverse order, the eyes, ears, heart. It is from the heart that corruption flows into the ears and eyes (Mar 7:21-22); but through the eyes and ears healing reaches the heart (Rom 10:17), [BENGEL]
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The three future clauses, with "lest" (pen), point back to these three imperatives in inverse order

notes.short: Wounds no one has dressed
notes.about: Isaiah speaks of the nation as one body, wounded from the sole of the foot to the head. Its wounds have not been cleansed, bandaged or soothed with oil: nothing has been done to heal it, and the people are left without relief.

figure.name: Metaphor
figure.words: neither cleansed nor bandaged nor soothed with oil
figure.means: Nothing has been done to heal the nation, pictured as a wounded body: it is left without relief or remedy.

notes.evidence: Calvin calls the three phrases metaphors, all meaning the nation is left without relief or remedy. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) sees the nation as one diseased body, with nothing applied to heal its wounds. Barnes: nothing was done toward healing, and the whole figure pictures the nation punished for its sins. Henry likens its sin to a diseased body: its unclosed wounds show no reform was tried.
notes.limit: Some take the wounds as the punishments the nation had already suffered, others as its sins left unrepented. Either way the picture shows a people no one has healed.

cites.quote: the three metaphors which he joins together ... have all the same meaning that the nation, without any hope of relief, without comfort, without remedy, is reduced to such a state of distress, that in such punishments the utmost severity of God is openly displayed.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: This description of the total misery of every individual in the nation is followed by a representation of the whole nation as one miserably diseased body. ... no means whatever had been applied to heal these many, various wounds
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The meaning is, that nothing had been done toward healing the wound. It was an unhealed, undressed, all-pervading sore. ... The whole figure in these two verses relates to their being punished for their sins.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: How he illustrates it by a comparison taken from a sick and diseased body, all overspread with leprosy ... No attempts were made for reformation, or, if they were, they proved ineffectual: The wounds have not been closed, not bound up, nor mollified with ointment.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: “Holy, holy, holy”: one word said three times
notes.about: The seraphim call out “holy” three times in a row. The repetition gives the word its fullest weight: the LORD is holy beyond measure, supremely holy. It can also be heard as praise that never tires, since His holiness gives it endless cause.

figure.name: Epizeuxis
figure.means: holiness of the highest degree, and praise of it that never ceases

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Epizeuxis: the LORD's holiness is stressed beyond measure, to the highest degree, and he sees the three Persons indicated. Barnes says the Hebrews repeated a word for the highest degree, so the words mean supremely holy. Henry hears the angels' fervent zeal and the surpassing excellence of God's holiness. Calvin reads it as the angels' unwearied, unceasing praise.
notes.limit: The writers stress different things: holiness beyond measure, or praise that never stops. Most of them also hear the three Persons of God in the threefold praise, though some say this verse alone does not prove it; the note does not rest on that.

cites.quote: The holiness of Jehovah is emphasized beyond measure, and the three persons in one God are indicated by the thrice repeated ... Here the highest degree of holiness is ascribed to Jehovah.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The Hebrews usually expressed the superlative degree by the repetition of a word. ... The form was used, therefore, among the Jews, to denote “emphasis;” and the expression means in itself no more than ‘thrice holy;’ that is, supremely holy.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: God's power was spoken twice ... but his holiness thrice, Holy, holy, holy. This bespeaks, [1.] The zeal and fervency of the angels in praising God; they even want words to express themselves, and therefore repeat the same again. ... [3.] The superlative excellency of God's holiness, above that of the purest creatures. He is holy, thrice holy, infinitely holy
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: And, indeed, this repetition rather points out unwearied perseverance, as if the Prophet had said, that the angels never cease from their melody in singing the praises of God, as the holiness of God supplies us with inexhaustible reasons for them.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: “All flesh is like grass”: frail and soon gone
notes.about: All mankind is called grass, and all its glory is likened to the flowers of the field. As grass withers and flowers fall, so people, with all their gifts and beauty, pass away. Verse 7 says it plainly: “the people are grass.” Against them stands the word of our God, which lasts forever (verse 8).

figure.name: Metaphor
figure.means: all people, weak and short-lived, who wither as grass does

original.note: In Hebrew the first line has no word for like; it says all flesh is grass. The second line has like, and Peter's Greek has it in both lines (1 Peter 1:24).

notes.evidence: Bullinger sets Peter's simile, all flesh as grass, beside Isaiah's metaphor, all flesh is grass. Barnes says all people are as weak and feeble as grass soon withered; Henry, that all flesh is grass, weak and withering, and its beauty soon blasted; Delitzsch, that men in the flesh are weak and perishing; Calvin, that man with all his gifts is compared to a flower that soon fades.
notes.limit: The writers read it of all mankind but apply it differently here: to Israel's oppressors, to Israel itself, or to no one nation in particular.

cites.quote: While the Simile says “All flesh is AS grass” (1Pe 1:24 ), the Metaphor carries the figure across at once, and says “All flesh IS grass” (Isa 40:6 ).
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: he states that all people are weak and feeble like the grass that is soon withered. ... Is grass - It is as feeble, weak, and as easily consumed as the grass of the field.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Of the vanity of the creature, that all flesh is grass, weak and withering. We ourselves are so, and therefore cannot save ourselves; all our friends are so, and therefore are unable to save us. All the beauty of the creature, which might render it amiable, is but as the flower of grass, soon blasted
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The appointed theme of his proclamation is the perishable nature of all flesh ... Men living in the flesh are universally impotent, perishing, limited ... Surely grass is the human race; such grass withereth and such flower fadeth
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: We ought carefully to observe that man, with his faculties, on account of which he is accustomed to value himself so highly, is wholly compared to a flower. ... But he shews that in man there is nothing so excellent as not to fade quickly and perish.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Know and understood around heard and declared
notes.about: Four questions go out and come back. The first and last ask about knowing and understanding, what can be learned by thinking on what God has made; the two in the middle ask about what had been heard and declared from the beginning.

lines.words: Do you not know?
Have you not heard?
Has it not been declared to you from the beginning?
Have you not understood since the foundation of the earth?

original.note: In Hebrew the first two verbs are futures, of what could be known, and the last two are perfects, of what has in fact been so.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) calls these four questions chiastically arranged: God may be known by reasoning or learned by what is handed down, and Israel shut itself off from both, from the knowledge open to it in a natural way and from the teaching that had come down from the beginning of its history.
notes.limit: The last question can also be read as insight into how the earth was founded; the BSB reads it as a time. Either way, know and understood stand around heard and declared.

cites.quote: four questions chiastically arranged. The absolute being of God … may be either inferred per ratiocinationem, or learned per traditionem. When Israel failed to acknowledge the absolute distinctness and unequalled supremacy of Jehovah its God, it hardened itself against the knowledge which it might acquire even in a natural way … and shut its ears against the teaching of revelation and tradition
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: “The arm of the LORD” stands for His power
notes.about: The LORD's arm stands for His power, the strength by which He acts. Here it is His saving power, made known in the Servant this chapter describes, yet few have seen it. John 12:38 applies the verse to the many who did not believe in Jesus.

figure.name: Anthropopatheia
figure.means: the LORD's power, here His saving power made known in grace

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Anthropopatheia: the LORD's arm makes known His grace in power. Barnes: the arm, an emblem of power, is God's power shown through the Messiah. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): power, shown in miracles and in saving men. Henry: the divine power that goes with the word. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch): almighty power that saves His people and exalts the Servant.
notes.limit: The writers agree the arm is God's power. They differ on where it is seen most: in the miracles that confirmed Christ's teaching, in the saving of sinners, or in the raising up of the Servant.

cites.quote: The Arm of the Lord is also used of the making known of His grace in wondrous power.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The arm is that by which we execute a purpose, and is often used as the emblem of power ... Here it denotes the omnipotence or power of God, which would be exhibited through the Messiah.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: arm--power ... exercised in miracles and in saving men ... "The arm of Jehovah" exhibited in Messiah while on earth.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: the arm of the Lord is not revealed to them; they do not discern, nor will be brought to acknowledge, that divine power which goes along with the word. The arm of the Lord is made bare ... in the miracles that were wrought to confirm Christ's doctrine
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: “We all like sheep have gone astray”
notes.about: The speakers confess that they are like sheep that have wandered off, each one turning to his own way. Sheep stray easily and cannot find the way home; so all had left God. The same verse says the LORD laid their iniquity on Him. Peter takes up the picture in 1 Peter 2:25.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: We all like sheep have gone astray
figure.means: people who have wandered from God, like sheep without a shepherd, each going his own way

notes.evidence: Bullinger gives these words as his example of a simile. Barnes says the race without a Redeemer is compared to a flock without a shepherd that wanders into every danger; Delitzsch, that Israel resembled a scattered flock without a shepherd; Henry, that we are like sheep, apt to wander and unable to find the way home.

cites.quote: The Simile says “All we like sheep,” while the Metaphor declares that “we are the sheep of His pasture.”
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The condition of the race without a Redeemer is here elegantly compared to a flock without a shepherd, which wanders where it chooses, and which is exposed to all dangers.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Israel in its exile resembled a scattered flock without a shepherd; it had lost the way of Jehovah
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: We have gone astray like sheep, which are apt to wander, and are unapt, when they have gone astray, to find the way home again. That is our true character
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Silent “as a sheep before her shearers”
notes.about: The Servant is compared to a lamb led to be killed and to a sheep silent before its shearers. Like them He goes without resisting or complaining, and does not open His mouth. In Acts 8:32-35 Philip begins from this passage to tell the good news about Jesus.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: led like a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is silent
figure.means: the Servant's willing, quiet bearing as He suffers, with no word of complaint

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse among his similes built on as and so. Delitzsch says the first simile shows His willing endurance and the second His quiet submission. Barnes: as a lamb led to be killed is patient and silent, so was He; Henry: His patience, His meekness and His cheerful yielding to His Father's will.

cites.quote: suffered; Lamb dumb, and so He; etc. (Isa 53:7 )
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The voluntary endurance is then explained by the simile "like a sheep that is led to the slaughter" (an attributive clause, like Jer 11:19 ); and the submissive quiet bearing, by the simile "like a lamb that is dumb before its shearers.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: This does not mean that he was led to the slaughter as a lamb is, but that as a lamb which is led to be killed is patient and silent, so was he. He made no resistance. ... As a sheep submits quietly to the operation of shearing.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: and as a sheep is dumb before the shearers, nay, before the butchers, so he opened not his mouth, which denotes not only his exemplary patience under affliction ... and his meekness under reproach ... but his cheerful compliance with his Father's will.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Thoughts, ways, then ways, thoughts
notes.about: Two words go out in one order and come back in the reverse order: thoughts, then ways in verse 8; ways, then thoughts in verse 9. Within verse 8, My and your also go out and come back reversed.

lines.words: For My thoughts are not your thoughts,
neither are your ways My ways,
For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so My ways are higher than your ways
and My thoughts than your thoughts.

notes.evidence: Bullinger sets out verse 8 as My thoughts, your thoughts, your ways, My ways, and says that verses 8 and 9 taken together are a simple Epanodos, the same words repeated in reverse order: thoughts, ways, ways, thoughts.

cites.quote: a “For my thoughts b are not your thoughts, b neither are your ways a my ways, saith the Lord.” … In verses 8 and 9 taken together, the figure is a simple Epanodos … Here in a and a we have “thoughts”; while in b and b we have “ways.”
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

notes.short: Mountains sing and trees clap their hands
notes.about: The mountains and hills are pictured singing, and the trees clapping their hands, as people do for joy. It shows the great joy of God's people as they go out and are led forth in peace. Some also read in it all creation sharing their freedom (Romans 8:21). Psalm 98:8 has a like picture.

figure.name: Personification
figure.words: the mountains and hills will burst into song before you, and all the trees of the field will clap their hands
figure.means: the great joy of God's people as they go out and are led forth in peace, as if all nature shared it

original.note: In Hebrew “hands” is kaph; in giving the trees hands, the prophet may have had in mind their branches, kippot.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Personification. Albert Barnes: lifeless things are pictured sharing the joy of God's people. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): nature's seeming sympathy, and its renewal. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch): the shouting and clapping are not literal, and creation will share the freedom of God's children. Plumptre (Ellicott): waving branches are like clapping hands.
notes.limit: All read the words as a picture of joy. Two also see in them the whole creation one day set free with God's people; the others do not say so.

cites.at: Prosopopoeia: human actions given to inanimate things, p. 866
cites.quote: “The mountains and the hills shall break forth before you into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands.” And thus is emphasised the universal joy of Israel in the coming day of her glory, when Jehovah shall comfort her.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Language like this is common in Isaiah, where all nature is called on to rejoice, or where inanimate objects are represented as expressing their sympathy with the joy of the people of God … Here it is an expression of the universal rejoicing which would attend the extension of the kingdom of God on the earth.

cites.quote: images justly used to express the seeming sympathy of nature with the joy of God's people. For, when sin is removed, the natural world shall be delivered from "vanity," and be renewed, so as to be in unison with the regenerated moral world
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: In applying the term kaph (hand) to the trees, the prophet had in his mind their kippōth, or branches. … That this transformation of the vegetation of the desert is not to be taken literally … is evident from the shouting of the mountains, and the clapping of hands on the part of the trees. … the whole creation will one day share in the liberty and glory of the children of God
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The waving of the branches of the trees is, in the poet’s thoughts, what the clapping of hands is with men, a sign of jubilant exultation
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: Your people possessed it; our enemies trample it
notes.about: The second line answers the first with its opposite. For a short while God's own people possessed His holy place; now enemies have trampled His sanctuary. The prayer sets the two side by side as a plea for God to act.

lines.words: For a short while Your people possessed Your holy place,
but our enemies have trampled Your sanctuary.

original.note: In Hebrew the second line turns the order round, so the two very different subjects, Your people and our enemies, meet in the middle of the verse.

notes.evidence: Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the words of the two clauses stand in reverse order, so that their two very different subjects touch in the middle, and the first verb looks further back than the second. Albert Barnes reads the verse as a plea: God's people possessed His sanctuary only a little time, and now His enemies trample it down.
notes.limit: What God's people held for a short while can be read as the holy land or as the temple itself.

cites.quote: The order of the words in the two clauses is chiastic. The two strikingly different subjects touch one another as the two inner members. Of the perfects, the first expresses the more remote past, the second the nearer past
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: As a reason for this, we urge that thy temple thy holy sanctuary - was possessed by thy people but a little time. For a brief period there we offered praise, and met with our God, and enjoyed his favor. Now thine enemies trample it down.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Heaven and earth are called on to listen
notes.about: Isaiah turns from the people and calls on the heavens and the earth to listen, as if they could hear the LORD's charge against His children. Some read it as a rebuke: the lifeless creation will listen sooner than God's own people.

figure.name: Apostrophe
figure.words: Listen, O heavens, and give ear, O earth
figure.means: heaven and earth, called as if they could hear, to witness the LORD's charge against His rebellious children

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Apostrophe to inanimate things. Calvin says the prophet turns to the dumb and lifeless elements because men have no ears. Henry says the prophet, despairing of a hearing from his people, speaks to the heavens and the earth. Barnes says heaven and earth are summoned as witnesses, in high poetic language that marks the weight of the matter.
notes.limit: One writer also offers a reading of heaven and earth as angels and the people of the world; others reject that reading and take them as the heavens and the earth themselves.

cites.quote: “Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth; for the Lord hath spoken.” These words were chosen for, and invariably put in, the title-page of the early printed editions of the English Bible.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: This is unquestionably a very severe protestation; for it conveys this meaning, that both turn to the elements which are dumb and devoid of feeling, because men have now no ears, or are bereft of all their senses. ... That no one may wonder at the circumstance of his addressing dumb and lifeless objects
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The prophet, though he speaks in God's name, yet, despairing to gain audience with the children of his people, addresses himself to the heavens and the earth, and bespeaks their attention ... Sooner will the inanimate creatures hear, who observe the law and answer the end of their creation, than this stupid senseless people.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: “Alas”: the prophet cries out over a sinful nation
notes.about: After charging the people in plain words, Isaiah cries out, “Alas, O sinful nation,” and heaps up names for a people weighed down by sin. Many hear in the cry both sorrow and indignation, for the people have forsaken the LORD and despised the Holy One of Israel.

figure.name: Exclamation
figure.means: sorrow and indignation at a people who have forsaken the LORD

original.note: In Hebrew “Alas” is hoy, a cry of pain that can also carry anger.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Ecphonesis, or Exclamation. Calvin calls it an exclamation of astonishment and sorrow that voices abhorrence; Henry says the prophet bemoans the people with holy indignation; Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) calls hoy a cry of pain, here a lament filled with wrath; Plumptre (Ellicott) hears in it indignation rather than pity.
notes.limit: The writers differ on the cry's chief note: most hear grief joined with indignation, but one hears indignation rather than pity.

cites.quote: So that Ecphonesis is an outburst of words, prompted by emotion, and is not used as though any reply were expected. ... “Ah sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, a seed of evil-doers, children that are corrupters.”
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: he adds an exclamation, by which he expresses still more strongly his abhorrence of such base ingratitude and wickedness. … it is an exclamation, suggested partly by astonishment, and partly by sorrow.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: He laments the universal pravity and corruption of their church and kingdom. … The prophet bemoans those that would not bemoan themselves: Alas for them! Woe to them! He speaks with holy indignation at their degeneracy, and a dread of the consequences of it.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Hoi is an exclamation of pain, with certain doubtful exceptions; and in the case before us it is not so much a denunciation of woe (vae genti, as the Vulgate renders it), as a lamentation (vae gentem) filled with wrath.

cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: Righteousness once lived in her; now murderers do
notes.about: Jerusalem's past is set against her present. Righteousness once made its home in the city, but now murderers live there in its place. Setting the two side by side makes the fall stark, for nothing is further from righteousness than murder.

figure.name: Antithesis
figure.words: righteousness resided within her, but now only murderers
figure.means: the righteousness that once lived in Jerusalem, set against the murderers who live there now

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Antithesis: murderers now lodge where righteousness lodged. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) calls the contrast most glaring, murder being the opposite of righteousness. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says the antithesis requires murderous oppressors. notes.short: Sent away, sold, then sold, sent away
notes.about: The first question asks about the mother who was sent away, the second about the children who were sold. The answer comes back to them in reverse order: you were sold for your iniquities, and for your transgressions your mother was sent away.

lines.words: Where is your mother’s certificate of divorce with which I sent her away?
Or to which of My creditors did I sell you?
Look, you were sold for your iniquities,
and for your transgressions your mother was sent away.

notes.evidence: Boys sets the verse out in four lines: the two central lines speak of selling into bondage and the two outer lines of divorce, two topics taken up again in reverse order.

cites.quote: Here the two central members relate to selling into bondage, and the two extreme ones to divorcement. The two topics are propounded in a. and b., and taken up, in an inverted order, in b. and a.

notes.short: Ears opened, back offered, face not hidden
notes.about: The lines go in threes and are built the same way: the Lord GOD has opened My ears, I have not been rebellious, nor have I turned back; I offered My back and My cheeks, and did not hide My face.

lines.words: The Lord GOD has opened My ears,
and I have not been rebellious,
nor have I turned back.
I offered My back to those who struck Me,
and My cheeks to those who tore out My beard.
I did not hide My face from scorn and spittle.

notes.short: Scorn and insults; moth and worm
notes.about: Each second line says the line before it again in other words: those who know what is right and have His law in their hearts, scorn and insults, the moth and the worm, His righteousness and His salvation.

lines.words: Listen to Me, you who know what is right,
you people with My law in your hearts:
Do not fear the scorn of men;
do not be broken by their insults.
For the moth will devour them like a garment,
and the worm will eat them like wool.
But My righteousness will last forever,
My salvation through all generations.

notes.about: Four words take turns. The first answers the third and the second the fourth, so devastation goes with famine and destruction with the sword.

do not be intimidated, for you will not be humiliated.

and will remember no more the reproach of your widowhood.

notes.short: Husband and Maker, Redeemer and Holy One, in turn
notes.about: Four lines take turns. The first answers the third: your husband is your Maker, and your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel. The second answers the fourth: the LORD of Hosts is His name, and He is called the God of all the earth.

lines.words: For your husband is your Maker
the LORD of Hosts is His name
the Holy One of Israel is your Redeemer;
He is called the God of all the earth.

notes.short: A moment of anger, everlasting kindness
notes.about: Each second line answers the line before it with its opposite. A brief moment of forsaking is set against great compassion, and anger that hid His face for a moment against everlasting kindness.

lines.words: For a brief moment I forsook you,
but with great compassion I will bring you back.
In a surge of anger I hid My face from you for a moment,
but with everlasting kindness I will have compassion on you,

notes.evidence: Barnes: the forsaking was little, the mercies great. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): everlasting, in contrast to a moment.

cites.quote: But with great mercies - The contrast here is not that of duration but of magnitude. The forsaking was 'little,' the mercies would be 'great.'

notes.short: Mountains may move; His devotion will not
notes.about: Four lines in two pairs, and the second pair answers the first with its opposite. The mountains may be removed and the hills shaken, but the LORD’s loving devotion will not depart and His covenant of peace will not be broken.

lines.words: Though the mountains may be removed
and the hills may be shaken,
My loving devotion will not depart from you,
and My covenant of peace will not be broken,

call on Him while He is near.
Let the wicked man forsake his own way
and the unrighteous man his own thoughts;
let him return to the LORD, that He may have compassion,
and to our God, for He will freely pardon.

notes.short: Foreigner, eunuch, then eunuchs, foreigners
notes.about: First the foreigner and then the eunuch are told what not to say. The LORD's promises answer them in reverse order, first to the eunuchs and then to the foreigners.

lines.words: Let no foreigner who has joined himself to the LORD say,
And let the eunuch not say,
To the eunuchs who keep My Sabbaths,
And the foreigners who join themselves to the LORD

notes.evidence: Boys puts the foreigners in the two parts he marks a and the eunuchs in the two he marks b. The foreigner and the eunuch are set before us in a and b, he says, and reading on, a promise is given first to the latter, the eunuch.

notes.short: Eggs, web, then eggs, web
notes.about: The lines take turns: the vipers' eggs and the spider's web, then the eggs again, deadly to eat and hatching a viper when cracked, and the web again, which cannot be made into clothing.

lines.words: They hatch the eggs of vipers
and weave a spider’s web.
Whoever eats their eggs will die;
Their cobwebs cannot be made into clothing,

notes.evidence: Boys sets these verses out in four members that take turns, the eggs in the first and third and the web in the second and fourth, each kept up in the later member.

cites.quote: In a. and a., the eggs; in b. and b., the web. The reference to the eggs in a. is kept up in the latter part of a., which speaks of crushing them; and the reference to the web in b., in the latter part of b., which speaks of a covering.

notes.short: Hoping for light, walking in darkness
notes.about: The people set what they hoped for against what came. They looked for light and found darkness, for brightness and walked in gloom. The light stands for the good days they waited to see return, and the darkness for the troubles that went on.

figure.name: Antithesis
figure.words: We hope for light, but there is darkness; for brightness, but we walk in gloom.
figure.means: the return of good days the people hoped for, set against the troubles that went on

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Antithesis. Henry reads it as hopes sadly disappointed: they waited for light as for the morning and saw no dawning of deliverance. Barnes takes the light as the prosperity they waited for and the darkness as calamities that went on, and Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) reads light as returning prosperity and obscurity as adversity.

cites.quote: “We wait for the light, but behold obscurity; For brightness, but we walk in darkness.”

cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Rising, light, glory, darkness, then back again
notes.about: Eight lines go out and come back. The call to arise answers the brightness of your dawn, your light answers your light, the glory of the LORD answers His glory, and the darkness over the earth and the peoples stands at the centre.

lines.words: Arise,
shine, for your light has come,
and the glory of the LORD rises upon you.
For behold, darkness covers the earth,
and thick darkness is over the peoples;
but the LORD will rise upon you, and His glory will appear over you.
Nations will come to your light,
and kings to the brightness of your dawn.

notes.evidence: Boys counts the three verses among his introverted forms, eight members in all: the rising in the first and last, the light in the second and seventh, the glory of the Lord in the third and sixth, and the darkness of mankind in the two at the centre.

cites.quote: In a. and a., the rising of the Church; in b. and b., its light; in c. and c., the glory of the Lord; in d. and d., the spiritual darkness of mankind. … these introverted forms. Here we have the most evident traces of art, contrivance, and design.

notes.short: “My servants will eat, but you will go hungry”
notes.about: Line after line, God sets what His servants will receive against what those who forsake Him will suffer: eating and hunger, drinking and thirst, joy and shame, a glad heart and a broken spirit. Set side by side, each fate makes the other stand out.

figure.name: Antithesis
figure.words: My servants will eat, but you will go hungry; My servants will drink, but you will go thirsty; My servants will rejoice, but you will be put to shame.
figure.means: the blessing God's servants will enjoy, set against the want and shame of those who forsake Him

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists verses 13 and 14 under Antithesis, as holding many antitheses. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the fates of the LORD's servants and of those who despise Him are announced in theses and antitheses. Barnes says the verse shows the difference between those who kept and those who forsook His commandments; Henry, that the two states are set against each other as a foil.

cites.quote: Where we have many beautiful Antitheses.

cites.quote: On the ground of the sin thus referred to again, the proclamation of punishment is renewed, and the different fates awaiting the servants of Jehovah and those by whom He is despised are here announced in five distinct theses and antitheses.
